newsitem.title: UK: Goldman's Davies says UK PSBR probably sustainable.
newsitem.headline: Goldman's Davies says UK PSBR probably sustainable.

text.p: Gavyn Davies, chief international economist at Goldman Sachs International, said Britain's public sector borrowing requirement (budget deficit) had improved significantly in recent years and was probably at sustainable levels.

Presenting the so-called Green Budget, in which the investment bank and the Institute for Fiscal Studies give their forecasts for the forthcoming budget, he said that even if the new Labour government did nothing, the deficit would improve under plans inherited from its Conservative predecessor.
"By the end of the parliament the tax burden will have increased, on our calculations, by 24 billion pounds per annum," Davies said.
"The budget deficit is probably sustainable. That's good news and it's against the trend of what most other people seem to be saying."

The higher tax burden would comprise seven billion stg of tax increases introduced by former Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke on items such as petrol and cigarettes and 17 billion stg in extra revenue due to real economic growth.
"Revenue is increasing by 2.0 percent of GDP over five years," Davies said.

Even if the new government were, contrary to all expectations and its own election promises, to dramatically increase public spending by 20 to 25 billion stg per year, the budget deficit would not get out of control.
"That would eliminate this budget surplus, but you would still end up with an approximately balanced budget because of this increase in government revenue," Davies said.
"Even if you take a relatively pessimistic view of the government's spending profile...they could get to a balanced budget by the end of the period."

Davies said corporation tax revenue was running around 3.5 billion stg ahead of expectations because of robust company profits while public spending would be 1.5 billion below expectations because of good GDP growth and low inflation.
The PSBR is expected to be 1.9 percent of GDP in 1997/98, down from the official government forecast in the November 1996 budget of 2.4 billion, dipping to 0.8 percent in 1998/99.
Davies said a sensible objective over the economic cycle would be a PSBR of one to 1.5 percent of GDP.
He did not believe a convincing case had been made for a substantial fiscal tightening in Labour's first budget this summer going beyond what was already in the pipeline.
